editorial.title: Capacity Exists, But How Much Can I Use Now?
editorial.dek: The global container fleet is bigger than ever. Yet effective capacity is shrinking.
body: The global container fleet is bigger than ever. There are ships in the water, containers in circulation and terminals operating. Yet effective capacity is shrinking.

Current port congestion is a useful example. More than 4.3 million TEU of container capacity is reportedly waiting to berth worldwide, exceeding the absolute congestion peak seen during the pandemic. East Asia is carrying much of that pressure, with large queues at Shanghai and Ningbo. Vessel delays are increasingly measured in days rather than hours.

A 15,000-TEU vessel sitting outside a port is still technically part of the global fleet. But while it waits, the ship falls behind schedule. Its next port call moves. Containers miss connections. Equipment stays in the wrong place. Another service begins operating with less usable capacity.

A major carrier has omitted a Shanghai call on one service after adverse weather affected the schedule, rerouting cargo to protect the onward rotation. That makes operational sense for the vessel, but the affected containers now require another solution.
What actually matters is usable capacity at the time and place where the cargo needs it.
Congestion, weather, security, equipment imbalance, missed connections and specialized cargo requirements all consume usable capacity.
The transportation asset does not have to disappear. It only has to stop being available when you need it.
The question, then, is not simply:
“How much capacity can I actually use, reliably, right now?”

items.title: Gulf ship traffic via Strait of Hormuz hovers below 10-day average, data shows
items.discovery: Middle East chokepoint and energy-shipping scan
items.summary: Only five commodity vessels transited Hormuz on August 25, versus a 10-day average of 15, Kpler data cited by Reuters showed. Iran and Oman are discussing a temporary joint shipping corridor and mine removal, but analysts caution that normal oil flows remain unlikely without broader political and sanctions changes.
items.logisticsImpact: Low transit confidence continues to constrain Gulf vessel availability, insurance appetite and schedule reliability. Corridor talks may improve access, but operators still face security, sanctions and route-risk decisions before flows normalize.

items.title: Global port congestion at new high as more typhoons hit China
items.summary: More than 4.3 million TEU is waiting to berth globally, with North Asia accounting for roughly half of the backlog. The Loadstar reports repeated typhoons are disrupting Chinese schedules while Durban is also congested because of equipment breakdowns, tightening effective vessel capacity across several trades.
items.logisticsImpact: Congestion removes usable capacity without removing ships from the fleet. Longer queues, missed rotations and equipment imbalance can extend transit times and keep transpacific rates and charter demand elevated.

items.title: China prepares for more heavy rain from back-to-back storms
items.discovery: East Asia weather and gateway-risk scan
items.summary: Typhoon Saudel is moving toward eastern China after affecting Okinawa, with Zhejiang and Fujian in the projected impact zone. The storm threatens gateways around Ningbo and Xiamen while regional networks are still recovering from earlier tropical systems and unusually heavy port congestion.
items.logisticsImpact: Fresh port, terminal, ferry, rail or trucking restrictions could deepen vessel queues and delay schedule recovery across Asia-Europe and transpacific networks, with equipment repositioning increasingly difficult.

items.title: Fire Breaks Out On Saudi Oil Tanker Near Red Sea Port Of Yanbu After Houthi Attack
items.summary: A tanker west of Yanbu was struck by a projectile and caught fire, with UKMTO reporting the incident and Bahri confirming its vessel Amzan was involved. The crew was reported safe. Claims about responsibility and weapon type remain subject to verification.
items.logisticsImpact: Security risk near Yanbu threatens a Red Sea export route used to reduce dependence on Hormuz, potentially raising war-risk premiums, voyage uncertainty and tanker-capacity costs.

items.title: India opens ports, airports to foreign-bound cargo impacted by Strait of Hormuz disruptions
items.discovery: South Asia customs and transshipment scan
items.summary: India is temporarily allowing foreign-bound cargo diverted by Hormuz disruption to unload, store and transship through its seaports and international airports. The customs facilitation covers containerized and specified bulk cargo under customs control and is scheduled to remain available through October 31.
items.logisticsImpact: The measure gives carriers and cargo owners an additional recovery option for stranded international cargo, reducing forced returns while creating new customs-controlled storage, onward-routing and transshipment choices through India.

items.title: Norway’s Digitoll customs rollout raises air cargo delay concerns
items.discovery: European customs and air-cargo compliance scan
items.summary: Norway’s first mandatory Digitoll phase begins September 15, requiring digital notification and cargo information before or at border crossing. Industry warnings say adoption remains low, particularly for air, sea and rail, raising the risk of border and cargo delays during the transition.
items.logisticsImpact: Forwarders, carriers and exporters moving freight into Norway need complete shipment data earlier in the process. Missing or late filings can hold time-critical cargo, shift compliance responsibility toward transport operators and create avoidable clearance delays.

items.title: Those behind hybrid attacks against Germany 'will pay,' Merz says, as officials find third drone at airport
items.summary: German investigators found another drone and suspected explosives linked to the earlier security incident around Leipzig/Halle Airport. The airport is a major European cargo and express hub, and previous activity around the site prompted diversions. Attribution remains under investigation.
items.logisticsImpact: Persistent drone or sabotage threats can trigger airfield stoppages, diversions and additional screening at a major express hub, affecting time-critical freight, parcel networks and specialized cargo operations.

items.title: Hormuz blockade causes project cargo build up
items.summary: Project-cargo carrier Chipolbrok says infrastructure and industrial cargo is building up as restrictions around Hormuz disrupt normal shipment planning. The backlog shows the Gulf disruption spreading beyond energy and container trades into multipurpose and heavy-lift movements.
items.logisticsImpact: Project cargo has limited substitution options for vessel type, lifting capacity and port handling. Backlogs can delay construction schedules, tie up specialized tonnage and increase storage, charter and financing costs.

items.title: US calls transhipments a 'scam': Why do firms reroute goods, and how does Singapore manage this?
items.summary: Growing U.S. scrutiny of tariff-evasion transshipment is focusing attention on major hubs including Singapore. The report highlights tighter origin analysis and the possibility of additional duties where authorities determine goods were routed through third countries to evade tariffs.
items.logisticsImpact: Importers and forwarders should expect more origin verification, manifest scrutiny and supplier-document reviews, especially for Chinese-origin inputs processed or routed through third countries before U.S. import.

items.title: ENGINE: East of Suez Fuel Availability Outlook (25 August 2026)
items.summary: Marine-fuel availability is tightening in parts of East of Suez markets, while typhoon-related weather has kept bunkering halted at Zhoushan outer anchorages. Singapore VLSFO availability was also reported tight, adding fuel-supply friction to already disrupted Asian vessel schedules.
items.logisticsImpact: Bunker delays and tighter prompt fuel availability can extend port stays, alter stem planning and force vessels to lift fuel elsewhere, adding cost and schedule pressure during a period of severe regional congestion.

items.title: dnata launches Cargo Integrated Command Centre to support million-tonne UAE operation
items.summary: dnata launched an integrated cargo command centre linking operational visibility across Dubai International and Al Maktoum International. The platform consolidates live operational data across a UAE cargo business that handled more than one million tonnes in the last financial year.
items.logisticsImpact: Better cross-airport visibility can improve exception management, labor allocation and transfer coordination for airlines and forwarders using Dubai during a period of continued Middle East network disruption.

items.title: Air China Cargo partners with cargo.one to debut e-booking for thousands of freight forwarders
items.discovery: Global air-cargo carrier and digital-booking scan
items.summary: Air China Cargo has made capacity available through cargo.one in its first global digital distribution partnership, initially opening e-booking access on key trade lanes from Europe and North America to China and beyond. The carrier combines a 24-freighter fleet with belly capacity across Air China’s passenger network.
items.logisticsImpact: Forwarders gain faster digital access to Air China Cargo pricing and capacity, reducing manual booking friction and broadening electronic procurement options on China-linked airfreight lanes.

items.title: LAUNCH OF THE NEW INDIA MIDDLE EAST MOMBASA (IMM) & INDIA MIDDLE EAST DAR ES SALAAM (IMD) SERVICE
items.discovery: Carrier network and East Africa connectivity scan
items.summary: ONE will launch two weekly services linking Nhava Sheva and Mundra with Mombasa and Dar es Salaam in September. The new rotations add direct India-East Africa capacity and provide another network option across trade lanes affected by wider Middle East routing uncertainty.
items.logisticsImpact: Additional direct sailings can reduce transshipment dependence and improve schedule options for India-East Africa cargo, particularly for shippers seeking alternatives while regional networks remain volatile.

items.title: Impala opens $20m mineral logistics hub at Port of Arica
items.discovery: Latin America port and bulk-logistics scan
items.summary: Impala Terminals opened a $20 million mineral handling and storage facility at Chile's Port of Arica, including an 11,100-square-metre warehouse, Rotainer containers and sealed truck transfers. The facility is intended to move Bolivian mineral storage away from the main port footprint.
items.logisticsImpact: Moving mineral storage outside the core terminal can free berth-side space, shorten handling cycles and expand Arica's capacity as a Pacific gateway for landlocked Bolivian trade.
